idiom_name: coarse operation methods over a remote interface, with transfer-object payloads and a client-side proxy
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: put a stateless service object at the boundary whose methods are named after use cases (placeOrder, quoteShipment) rather than after fields; each method does three things only - translate the request payload into calls on fine-grained objects, run the use case, and translate the result back into a transfer object. The fine-grained objects keep local interfaces and never appear in a remote method signature. On the client side a generated or hand-written proxy wraps marshalling and the transport call so callers see an ordinary object. Keep the facade free of domain logic, and make its operations idempotent where the transport may retry.
code_sketch:
class OrderFacade:                       # remote interface, no domain logic
    def place_order(self, req: PlaceOrderRequest) -> OrderConfirmation: ...
    def fetch_order_summary(self, req: OrderIdRequest) -> OrderSummary: ...

class OrderFacadeImpl(OrderFacade):
    def place_order(self, req):
        order = Order.create(req.customer, req.lines)   # fine-grained objects
        pricing = repo.pricing_for(order)
        return OrderConfirmation.from(order, pricing)   # transfer object
# client: proxy = RemoteProxy(OrderFacade, channel); proxy.place_order(req)
pitfalls: Returning live domain entities from the facade: the object graph then leaks across the boundary and the pattern degenerates into distributed objects.
Putting domain logic in the facade; it must translate and delegate, or the model is split across the boundary.
One coarse method per screen instead of per use case, which produces a broad, unstable surface and duplicated orchestration.

Wrong move: hide every remote call behind local-looking entity methods -> Y fails because latency, retries and partial failures stay invisible -> instead expose a bounded use-case operation with explicit deadlines, idempotency and failure semantics.

Wrong move: assume a batch is atomic by default -> Y fails when subrequests have independent or dependency-specific outcomes -> instead document transaction scope and return per-item results, or require an explicit all-or-none contract.

Wrong move: mirror screens or database tables in facade methods -> Y fails because clients couple to unstable presentation or storage details -> instead derive a small versioned operation from a cohesive use case.
